sections.title: A planned city on a vast scale
sections.body: Teotihuacan stands in a valley north-east of modern Mexico City. Its broad ceremonial avenue, pyramids and residential compounds reveal a settlement organised through extensive construction and planning. The impressive monuments were part of a much larger urban environment, with neighbourhoods and working areas beyond the most photographed buildings. Studying only the pyramids would leave out much of the city's social and economic history.

sections.title: Architecture and meaning
sections.body: The Pyramids of the Sun and Moon and the Temple of the Feathered Serpent are connected by a carefully arranged urban plan. Decorated buildings and painted walls provide evidence of artistic traditions and religious ideas, but many questions about the city's government and beliefs remain disputed. Its modern name comes from later Nahua tradition, so it should not be mistaken for a precise record of how its inhabitants named their own city.

sections.title: A major centre of exchange
sections.body: Teotihuacan influenced communities well beyond its valley through trade, imagery and social connections. The presence of materials and styles from different regions helps researchers investigate those links. The city's later decline and abandonment were complex processes, not one fully explained disaster. Archaeology continually changes interpretations of who lived here and how a large population was supplied and organised.

sections.title: What the ground plan reveals
sections.body: A map makes the ceremonial axis and surrounding neighbourhoods easier to understand than a close photograph of one monument. The city's relationship with waterways and valley terrain also mattered. Teotihuacan offers a view of sophisticated urbanism in ancient Mesoamerica while reminding visitors that much of ordinary life remains harder to reconstruct than spectacular architecture.

records.quickFact: The pyramids are only part of a much wider planned ancient city.

records.focus: Coiba National Park and Marine Protection Zone
records.hook: Panama — Coiba National Park and Marine Protection Zone

sections.title: Islands off the Pacific coast
sections.body: Coiba lies in the Gulf of Chiriquí off Panama's Pacific coast, surrounded by smaller islands and protected marine waters. Its isolation helped sustain distinctive forest habitats, while the sea around it belongs to a wider eastern Pacific ecological network. The World Heritage property includes land and ocean environments rather than an island viewed separately from its surrounding water.

sections.title: Endemism and ecological connections
sections.body: Species living on islands can develop different traits and populations when isolated from their mainland relatives. Coiba's forests are therefore valuable for studying ecological change, while reefs and offshore waters support fish, marine mammals and other animals whose movements cross park boundaries. The protected marine zone illustrates why conservation cannot stop at a shoreline, especially where animals travel considerable distances.

sections.title: A complicated human history
sections.body: Coiba was used as a penal colony for much of the twentieth century, a past that is separate from the older histories of Panama's Pacific coast. Closure and changing management altered access to the island. Conservation and research now shape its public identity, but protecting habitats also requires monitoring tourism and marine resource use. The island's history should not be romanticised as a permanently empty paradise.

sections.title: See the ecosystem as a whole
sections.body: A mangrove edge, tropical forest and offshore feeding area can be connected through nutrients and animal movements. Conditions vary across the archipelago, and scientific work continues to reveal those relationships. Coiba is a strong example of island ecology and of the difficulties of protecting environments linked to a much larger ocean system.

records.quickFact: Coiba protects both island forests and marine routes used by Pacific wildlife.

records.focus: Jesuit Missions of Trinidad and Jesús de Tavarangue
records.hook: Paraguay — Jesuit Missions of Trinidad and Jesús de Tavarangue

sections.title: Two mission settlements
sections.body: The remains of La Santísima Trinidad de Paraná and Jesús de Tavarangue belong to the history of Jesuit missions established in the Río de la Plata region. Their buildings formed parts of larger settlements rather than isolated churches. Surviving masonry and street arrangements give clues to religious life, workshops and the organisation of daily activities during the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.

sections.title: Indigenous lives and colonial power
sections.body: The missions involved Guaraní communities and European Jesuit clergy within changing colonial systems. Their history includes cultural exchange, adaptations in art and settlement practices, and unequal power relationships. It would be inaccurate to present the sites merely as successful architecture or to imply that Indigenous people played a passive role. The structures offer evidence for examining both community activity and colonial control.

sections.title: A wider regional network
sections.body: Related settlements developed across areas now divided between Paraguay, Argentina and Brazil. Rivers and overland routes enabled communication and exchange, while political decisions reshaped the system over time. The architecture combined techniques and artistic influences in distinctive ways. Today the surviving missions belong to different national jurisdictions, although their historical connections crossed modern borders.

sections.title: What remains to investigate
sections.body: Some buildings survive only in partial form, and conservation must stabilise stonework without inventing missing features. A church wall or courtyard outline reveals just one part of the former settlement. These Paraguayan sites invite questions about religion, labour, Indigenous agency and the way colonial institutions altered landscapes that already had long human histories.

records.quickFact: The surviving mission layouts belong to a network that once extended across three present-day countries.

sections.title: Plateaus above the forest
sections.body: South-eastern Venezuela contains immense table-like mountains known as tepuis. Canaima National Park protects extensive examples of these ancient rock formations, with vertical cliffs, river systems and broad forested landscapes. Their forms result from long geological histories of rock uplift and erosion. The appearance of isolated summits makes them memorable, but the wider park includes many habitats beyond a single dramatic waterfall.

sections.title: Water and ancient rock
sections.body: Rainfall feeds streams that run across plateau surfaces before descending steep escarpments. Waterfalls and dark-water rivers connect high rock environments with lower forests and savannah areas. The sandstone and quartzite geology helps explain both the shapes of landforms and the often nutrient-poor conditions affecting vegetation. The park is a landscape of hydrological relationships, not simply a collection of sightseeing locations.

sections.title: Life on isolated summits
sections.body: Some plants and other organisms have highly restricted ranges associated with separate tepui environments. That makes the region important for biodiversity research, while changing climate and human activity raise difficult conservation questions. The park also lies within lands of Indigenous communities, including Pemón peoples, whose histories and knowledge must not be omitted from descriptions of the environment.

sections.title: A place requiring care
sections.body: Remoteness does not mean a landscape is free of social or environmental pressures. Park management involves access, livelihoods and threats to habitats. When studying Canaima, compare the open summit rock with surrounding forest and waterways. The contrast shows how isolation and geological structure can shape ecology across short distances.

records.quickFact: Canaima's tepuis support distinctive life above extensive forest and river landscapes.

sections.title: A Maya centre in a river valley
sections.body: Copán lies in western Honduras, where the ruins of a major Maya city occupy part of a wider valley landscape. Plazas, ceremonial buildings and carved monuments survive as evidence of political and religious activity. The site developed over several centuries and belonged to a network of Maya centres with relationships across what are now national borders. Its importance cannot be understood from a single pyramid.

sections.title: History written in stone
sections.body: Inscribed stelae and architectural programmes record aspects of dynastic history, while the Hieroglyphic Stairway is an extraordinary archaeological resource. Research has helped interpret some rulers, events and artistic conventions, though evidence remains incomplete. Studying such texts requires specialist knowledge, and not every building or carved figure has an agreed interpretation. Maya history is a living field of scholarship, not a solved puzzle.

sections.title: People beyond the monuments
sections.body: Residential remains and studies of the wider settlement help archaeologists examine households, farming and the practical organisation of the valley. Monumental centres relied on people whose names are rarely preserved in inscriptions. Modern Maya communities continue to exist in the wider region; describing the civilisation as simply vanished would misrepresent that continuity.

sections.title: Conserving a fragile record
sections.body: Weathering, vegetation and visitor pressure can affect carved stone and exposed ruins. Excavation reveals evidence but can also expose material to new risks. Copán offers a way to connect writing, art, urban planning and landscape archaeology. Its central monuments are impressive, but the strongest interpretation considers how they related to the whole society around them.

records.quickFact: Copán's inscriptions and Hieroglyphic Stairway help reconstruct parts of Maya political history.

sections.title: An island with several histories
sections.body: Robben Island lies offshore from Cape Town and was used for different institutional purposes over centuries, including imprisonment, military activities and medical isolation. The buildings remaining today belong to several periods, so it should not be described as though its history began in the twentieth century. The island's most widely recognised significance, however, comes from the struggle against apartheid.

sections.title: Political imprisonment and resistance
sections.body: The maximum-security prison held political prisoners under the apartheid system, including Nelson Mandela. Its history is inseparable from state repression and efforts to establish democratic rights. Former prisoners' testimony is important to interpretation because buildings alone cannot explain the personal, political and social meaning of imprisonment. Visitors should approach the site as a place of historical learning and remembrance.

sections.title: The island's physical setting
sections.body: Water separated the island from the mainland, shaping access and control. Quarries, residential and administrative buildings and coastal infrastructure remain as material evidence of different uses. Environmental conditions affect conservation and how visitors move through the site. The landscape is also home to wildlife and vegetation, but that natural setting should not distract from the experiences being commemorated.

sections.title: Why the site matters today
sections.body: Robben Island is part of a wider South African history of resistance, inequality and democratic change. It cannot stand alone as an explanation of apartheid or the work of everyone who opposed it. The island allows people to examine how political systems used confinement and how those subjected to oppression sustained movements for change, while recognising the responsibility to preserve reliable historical evidence.

records.quickFact: Robben Island preserves evidence of political imprisonment and South Africa's struggle against apartheid.

sections.title: A highland forest in the Albertine Rift
sections.body: Nyungwe lies in south-western Rwanda within the biodiverse Albertine Rift. Its forest landscape includes high-altitude habitats, wet ground, open vegetation and contrasting smaller environments. Variation in slope, rainfall and elevation creates conditions for many different species. The park's UNESCO property includes several forest components and illustrates why the region is important for conservation beyond any one national boundary.

sections.title: Species with specialised habitats
sections.body: Primates, birds, amphibians and plants depend on the forest's different environments. Eastern chimpanzees are among the best-known inhabitants, but they are only one part of a highly complex community. Some species found here have restricted distributions, which can make habitat changes particularly consequential. Scientific monitoring is valuable precisely because much of the biodiversity is not easily visible to visitors.

sections.title: People and forest protection
sections.body: The forest sits within a region where communities have long depended on land, water and other resources. Modern conservation involves questions about livelihoods, access, tourism and landscape management. Treating the park as an empty wilderness would ignore those relationships. Researchers and local institutions must also consider how habitat connections can be maintained amid land-use changes beyond protected boundaries.

sections.title: A water and climate perspective
sections.body: Mountain forests influence how rainfall moves through vegetation and soil before reaching streams and rivers. Different altitudes produce changes in plant cover and microclimates. Nyungwe is a useful case study of the relationship between highland geology, ecological diversity and conservation decisions, not simply a destination for spotting primates.

records.quickFact: Nyungwe protects different highland forest habitats within the Albertine Rift biodiversity region.

sections.title: A mountain tied to memory
sections.body: Le Morne Brabant stands on Mauritius's south-western coast, rising above the Indian Ocean. Its rugged cliffs and relatively isolated terrain made parts of the mountain difficult to reach. The physical setting is central to the site's historical meaning, because it became associated with people escaping slavery. The landscape should be understood through those human experiences rather than only through dramatic mountain photography.

sections.title: Maroons and resistance
sections.body: Escaped enslaved people, often called maroons, sought places of refuge where they could avoid capture. Le Morne became an important symbol of their resistance and pursuit of freedom. Archaeological evidence and oral traditions help explain that history, although every detail of the stories cannot be established with equal certainty. Respectful interpretation distinguishes well-supported evidence from later traditions while recognising the importance of both.

sections.title: An island in oceanic networks
sections.body: Mauritius was connected to extensive systems of migration, trade and forced labour across the Indian Ocean. The origins and experiences of the island's communities cannot be reduced to one background. Le Morne provides a focal place for examining the effects of slavery within a wider regional history that connected Africa, Asia and European colonial powers.

sections.title: Preservation and public understanding
sections.body: The site's value is partly intangible: memory, identity and the meanings attached to the mountain matter alongside the rock itself. Conservation must consider development, access and the views of descendant communities. The most revealing question is how a difficult natural landscape became a place of refuge and then an enduring national symbol of freedom.

records.quickFact: Le Morne's terrain is inseparable from histories and memories of escape from slavery.

sections.title: A trading island off the coast
sections.body: The Island of Mozambique lies near the northern Mozambican coast, with a historic town shaped by centuries of Indian Ocean exchange. Maritime networks connected East Africa with Arabia, India and later European trading powers. Fortifications, religious buildings, streets and houses preserve evidence of those links. Its urban landscape cannot be explained solely as a European colonial settlement because older and continuing regional influences are equally significant.

sections.title: Two contrasting built traditions
sections.body: The island contains areas traditionally associated with stone-and-lime buildings and other neighbourhoods with local macuti-roofed housing. Their differences reveal varied materials, building practices and social histories. Structures changed under Portuguese rule, but their forms also reflect African, Swahili and Indian Ocean connections. The UNESCO property recognises the built landscape as a whole rather than a single fort or church.

sections.title: Life in a narrow coastal setting
sections.body: Water supply, sanitation, housing and the maintenance of historic buildings pose practical problems on a small island. The same coastal setting that once helped maritime trade can complicate modern infrastructure. Conservation is therefore closely linked with residents' needs. Emptying a place of everyday life in order to preserve photographs would miss much of its historical meaning.

sections.title: Look beyond the fort
sections.body: Streets, small houses and waterfront activities provide clues to the island's role in wider trade networks. The history involves merchants, sailors, craftspeople and people affected by colonial domination. Buildings preserve some of that evidence, but their present condition also reveals the continuing work required to conserve a living historic town.

records.quickFact: The island's architecture combines East African and Indian Ocean traditions with later colonial forms.

sections.title: A former capital at a river junction
sections.body: Ayutthaya developed as a major Siamese capital on an island enclosed by river channels. Its position supported commerce and defence, while the waterways also shaped planning and transport. From the fourteenth to eighteenth centuries the city became a centre of political authority and exchange. The surviving ruins include temples and towers, but the historic capital was much more than its ceremonial structures.

sections.title: Architecture and regional networks
sections.body: Monasteries and distinctive prang towers reveal artistic and religious traditions alongside influences moving through diplomacy and trade. International merchants and envoys visited the city, which connected inland Southeast Asia with maritime routes. The archaeology must be interpreted with surviving written accounts and plans. It would be misleading to think that the ruined buildings show the whole population or every part of city life.

sections.title: The consequences of destruction
sections.body: In 1767 the city suffered a major attack and destruction, and the capital did not return to the same site. Later activities and excavation changed what could be seen. The ruins still reveal the scale of earlier urban planning, including roads, canals and defences, but loss of structures complicates reconstruction. Archaeologists work with what survives rather than restoring an imagined perfect capital.

sections.title: Water management remains central
sections.body: Ayutthaya's history is tied to managing rivers and seasonal floods. Studying the waterways helps explain its foundation, prosperity and vulnerabilities. The site offers an example of urban engineering as well as cultural heritage, showing how political centres depend on physical landscapes and the systems people build to work within them.

records.quickFact: Ayutthaya's river-island position was central to its trade, defence and urban planning.

sections.title: A trade network across southern Arabia
sections.body: The Land of Frankincense links several heritage locations in the Dhofar region of Oman. Trees producing aromatic resin, inland routes and coastal ports were connected by a trade that operated across long periods. Rather than one monument, the World Heritage property includes parts of an economic system. The landscape ranges from valleys and oases to coastal settlements whose roles depended on wider markets.

sections.title: From tree to caravan
sections.body: Frankincense comes from the resin of particular Boswellia trees. Collection and transport required knowledge of local growing conditions and routes through demanding terrain. Inland places such as Shisr helped connect production areas with longer-distance caravans, while ports linked goods with maritime journeys. The story is one of practical geography and commercial organisation rather than a single legendary incense road.

sections.title: Coastal history and exchange
sections.body: Khor Rori and Al Baleed preserve evidence of settlements involved in Indian Ocean and Arabian trade. Their buildings and archaeological remains reveal changing periods of regional activity. Merchants, workers and communities exchanged goods and ideas; those interactions shaped the coast over centuries. The surviving ruins must be studied carefully because each site had different functions and chronological phases.

sections.title: A connected heritage landscape
sections.body: Desert and coastal conditions affect the preservation of archaeology and the management of visitors. Conservation includes the trees and places of production as well as forts, ports and urban remains. The strongest way to understand this property is to follow the full chain of collection, inland movement and shipping rather than viewing the sites independently.

records.quickFact: Frankincense production linked Oman’s Dhofar valleys to inland caravans and ocean trade.

sections.title: A port on a volcanic island
sections.body: Levuka sits along the coast of Ovalau Island in Fiji, with forested slopes rising sharply behind the town. Its historic street pattern developed between the shoreline and the island's terrain. Buildings along the waterfront record the growth of a nineteenth-century trading centre that later became Fiji's first colonial capital. The narrow site helps explain why sea access and coastal routes were so important.

sections.title: Local communities and colonial contact
sections.body: Indigenous Fijian settlements existed in the area as European and American traders established businesses and institutions. The town's buildings and layout reflect these encounters, but the period cannot be described simply as harmonious exchange. Colonial rule involved unequal political power and major changes to the islands' economy and society. Levuka's heritage requires attention to Indigenous experiences alongside the surviving commercial and government architecture.

sections.title: The architecture of a working town
sections.body: Warehouses, religious buildings, homes and public facilities were built using varied materials and techniques. Their low-rise forms contrast with the surrounding volcanic slopes, making the port town's relationship with landscape clear. When the capital moved to Suva, Levuka remained a settlement with its own industries and community life. Surviving buildings represent several phases rather than an untouched moment in time.

sections.title: Protecting a lived-in place
sections.body: Historic waterfront structures can face weathering and development pressures, while residents need functioning infrastructure and services. Conservation works best when it respects the town as a community rather than turning it into an outdoor display. Levuka offers a view of Pacific maritime history and how local and colonial building traditions shaped a distinctive urban setting.

records.quickFact: Levuka's preserved waterfront records the encounter of Indigenous settlements and colonial port development.
